utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] I should like to ask the Prosecution to introduce itself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mr. David Re on my far right-hand side, Mr. Daryl Mundis behind me, the case manager is Mrs. Kimberly Fleming, and my name is Mr. Ekkehard Withopf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me now ask the Defence to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for General Enver Hadzihasanovic. My co-counsel is Stephane Bourgon, attorney from Montreal. And with us is our legal assistant, Mirna Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Mr. Rodney Dixon, and Mr. Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could the accused stand, please. I wish to ask Mr. Hadzihasanovic to introduce himself, to tell us his first and last name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Enver Hadzihasanovic. I was born on the 7th of July, 1950 in Zvornik. I am living in Sarajevo, Trampina Street number 6. I am a general of the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, retired as of 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KUBURA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Amir Kubura, born on the 4th of March, 1964, municipality of Kakanj in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am an officer of the army of the Federation. I am living in Sarajevo, Topalosmana Street, number 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Let me first address the two accused before giving the floor to the Prosecutor. Regarding the accused, I am going to tell you'll that there will be an opening statement presented by the Prosecutor. If you wish, you may make a statement after that. That statement will not be subject to any questions. In continuation of the proceedings, regarding the production of evidence by the Prosecution, the Prosecution will be presenting its evidence principally through witnesses. The witnesses will be examined first by the Prosecutor, who will be conducting the examination-in-chief, and then the Defence may engage in a cross-examination. If necessary, the Prosecutor may re-examine the witness. The cross-examination will be under the control of the Judges of this Chamber. The cross-examination must be limited to the subjects covered by the examination-in-chief to questions that may affect the credibility of the witness, and questions that have to be relevant in relation to the evidence of the party that is cross-examining, and it is only with the permission of the Judges that other questions may possibly be put. When the Prosecutor has completed the presentation of its evidence - and we believe that that will be around the month of June next year - the accused may, if they so wish, file a motion of acquittal. This is envisaged by Rule 88 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I beg correction -- 98 bis. In that case, the Chamber, if it so considers that there is sufficient evidence to rule acquittal, it may do so. Otherwise, it will then be the case, the turn of the Defence to present its evidence. And within that framework, you will be able to make an opening statement if you so wish. You may call witnesses to testify, and you may present other forms of evidence. You may also, if you wish, appear as witnesses within the framework of your own defence. All the witnesses called by the Defence - and yourself, if you wish to testify - will then be cross-examined by the Prosecution. After this stage, we will come to the rebuttal evidence. The Prosecutor may call witnesses to testify to rebut the evidence presented by the Defence. The accused may also be authorised to call its own witnesses in response. Also, the Chamber may call witnesses if it considers that to be necessary. So after this stage, we will come to the pleadings, and in accordance with the Rules of Evidence they will submit their briefs and the Judges of the Chamber will hear the arguments and pleas of the Prosecution and of the Defence, upon which the Judges will deliberate and pronounce judgement in a public hearing on a date that will be decided by the Judges. The procedure that I have now summarised is envisaged by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in Rules 84 onwards. You have the Rules at your disposal, and you were able to consult the relevant articles and rules dealing with the proceedings themselves. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecutor to make his opening statement, having noted that last Friday the Chamber invited the parties to get in touch in order to make progress regarding the points of law and fact on which they agree or disagree, and I believe that today or tomorrow we will have a written document reflecting the outcome of the meetings that you held yesterday. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecution to make its opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a case about command responsibility. It is a case about the criminal liability of the two accused, Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura, General Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Kubura for failing to prevent and failing to punish crimes, war crimes committed by their subordinates. It is the first pure command responsibility case in the history of this Tribunal. It is the first trial of military commanders for criminal responsibility purely based on their subordinates' conduct. And it is a case that shows the flip side to a number of cases that have been tried by this Tribunal. The most prominent are the cases the Prosecutor versus Blaskic and the Prosecutor versus Kordic and Cerkez. As such, this trial against Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura demonstrates - demonstrates - that all sides to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, although in different areas and different in scale, committed the serious violations of international humanitarian law that fall under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. On 3 March 2000, Your Honours, the Tribunal's then-President, Judge Jorda, foreshadowed this in delivering the judgement in the Blaskic case. He stated that - and I'm quoting - "The Trial Chamber has taken note of the possibility that crimes were committed by Muslim forces." And he went on to say, "The Trial Chamber considers -- considers that it has received evidence of atrocities committed against Croatian civilians and that the then-perpetrators of those crimes must be prosecuted. This is the trial of the commanders whose soldiers, whose subordinates, committed some of those atrocities. This trial will contribute to our understanding of what happened in Central Bosnia in 1993. The evidence will show that the other side of the war crimes prosecuted in the Blaskic, Kordic and Cerkez, and Kupreskic cases, it will show that war crimes were being committed -- were committed by both sides of the conflict in Central Bosnia. This trial will give the world a more complete picture of the war in Bosnia. I will now very briefly turn to the military and political situation in Central Bosnia that resulted in the conflict between the army of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ABiH, and the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO. The background against which this conflict started, the reasons for it, the military and the political developments in the course of this conflict, have been the subject matter -- have been the subject matter of a number of trials before this Tribunal. Accordingly these facts have been repeatedly - repeatedly have been addressed in Tribunal's judgements. They are well known and they merit only a brief summary. The former Yugoslavia was comprised of six republics and two autonomous regions. In the late 1980s and in the early 1990s, social and political events culminated within the disintegration of that state. Four of the republics - namely, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, and Macedonia - declared their independence. In the wake of such declarations of independence, terrible and horrible wars, bloody wars ensued, particularly in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Focussing on the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the parties to the conflict were generally -- were generally, although not exclusively, divided amongst ethnic lines. The Bosnian Serbs, supported by the Yugoslav army, the JNA, attempted to create an independent -- an independent entity known as the Republika Srpska. They were opposed by the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, both groups, the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats were initially under the direction of the central government in Sarajevo. Whilst the Bosnian Serbs made significant -- significant territorial gains and seized control over large parts of the country, the original alliance between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims against the Serbian offensive fell apart. It fell apart in Central Bosnia. A war within a war, the Muslim-Croat war erupted. As a result, between January 1993 and March 1994, the ABiH on the one side and the HVO, supported by the army of the Republic of Croatia, the HV, on the other side, engaged in an armed conflict in Central Bosnia. This armed conflict continued -- continued throughout the time relevant to this indictment. That were and the war crimes committed by troops of the ABiH subordinated to the two accused are the subject of the indictment. I will now turn to the command structure within the ABiH 3rd Corps. In order to assist the Trial Chamber, we will show a number of maps that will give an impression of the geographical locations where the crimes -- where the crimes by the subordinates of the two accused were committed. By a presidential decree of 18 August 1992, the ABiH was divided into five military areas of responsibility known as corps. The areas -- the five areas of responsibility are detailed on the first map we are about to show you now. You have the 3rd Corps, covering substantial periods -- substantial portions, as you can see on the map, of Central Bosnia, the 3rd Corps located between the 5th Corps in the west and the 2nd Corps in the east, covering areas of Central Bosnia located to the north of Sarajevo. Due to the fact that the Bosnian Serbs had occupied substantial portions of its geographical area, in particular to the north, as one can see from the confrontation line, which is detailed on the map, the 3rd Corps temporary headquarter was based in Zenica. It was based in Zenica throughout the indictment period. The 3rd Corps area under the control of the ABiH covered, as can also be seen from the map - from the next map; it's map number 3 - covered a number of municipalities, including the ones in which subordinates of the accused committed the crimes. Such municipalities include the municipality of Bugojno, the municipality of Travnik, Zenica, Kakanj, and Vares. Such municipalities, these municipalities are detailed on the map, Your Honours, you have in front of you. From 14th November 1992, the accused Hadzihasanovic, General Hadzihasanovic, commanded the 3rd Corps. At the time he took over command, he had already served for more than 20 years in the JNA. Having completed the Belgrade land forces military academy and subsequently the staff officers college in Belgrade, and having been assigned to a number of different command positions within the JNA, the accused Hadzihasanovic in 1993, he was an experienced military commander. And we already wish to now -- we already now wish to draw your attention to the fact that the accused Hadzihasanovic, as a long-serving JNA military police officer, had gained substantial - substantial - experience in respect to prevent and to punish crimes, inclusive crimes of such nature, which are the subject matter of this indictment. Turning to the accused Kubura. From 1 April 1993, the accused Kubura, first as acting commander until 20 July 1993, and from 21st July 1993 onwards as its appointed commander, commanded the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Like the accused Hadzihasanovic, also the accused Kubura at the time he took over command, was an experienced -- an experienced professional military officer within the JNA. In 1992, he had already been assigned command positions within the ABiH, first as a deputy commander of a detachment in Kakanj, and subsequently as the commander of a mountain battalion in the same area. When he took over -- when the accused Kubura took over his command position as acting commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade, Your Honours, this brigade was already well known to him. It was well known to him because already on 11th December 1992 he was assigned as its assistant chief of staff for operations and instruction matters. Only a few weeks later, on 1st January 1993, he was appointed chief of staff, a position he held until he was appointed the acting commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. The Prosecution's military expert, Dr. Reinhardt, a retired NATO general, who also served as a commander of KFOR in Kosovo has examined hundreds of orders, literally hundreds of orders, communications, and reports from within the 3rd Corps during the indictment period. His expert opinion -- his expert opinion is that clear and effective lines of subordination existed in the 3rd Corps between the corps commander and the subordinate commanders, such as Kubura. His opinion, his expert opinion is that the accused Hadzihasanovic exercised effective control over his subordinates, including the accused Kubura, and that the accused Kubura exercised effective control over his subordinates in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. I will now turn to the indictment itself. Between January 1993 and January 1994, soldiers of the ABiH 3rd Corps committed numerous - numerous - violations of laws and customs of war, including breaches of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions of 1949. The indictment contains seven counts; all concern violations of the laws or customs of war. The underlying crimes, Your Honours, the underlying crimes - and there are more than 20 - include murder, cruel treatment, wanton destruction of cities, towns, and villages not justified by military necessity, plunder and destruction or willful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion. Victims of these crimes -- victims were mainly Bosnian Croats, both HVO soldiers and civilians. Bosnian Serbs were to a minor extent also victims. The count on willful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion is charged only against the accused Hadzihasanovic. Moreover, there are some alleged crimes in specific locations, such as those aspects of Count 1, relating to Dusina that apply only to the accused Hadzihasanovic. The war crimes alleged include three incidents -- three incidents of execution and massacre-type of murders, crimes, cruel treatment, and again murders committed in 12 detention facilities in four municipalities, crimes of plunder and wanton destruction of six towns and villages in three municipalities, and the willful damage of two churches - the monastery in Guca Gora and one church in Travnik. The next map, Your Honours, we are about to show you now shows the locations, the locations where all these crimes were committed. As can be seen from this map, subordinates of both accused committed crimes in various -- in various areas in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility. Most prominent is the area of the Bila Valley [phoen] between the towns of Travnik in the west and Zenica in the east. This area is located to the north-west of Zenica. Several -- several of the names of the villages, as detailed on this map, Your Honours, Maline, Bikosi, Mehurici, Miletici and Orosac, in the areas just mentioned, and Dusina in the south-west of Zenica, became synonyms -- became synonyms for brutal crimes. Brutal crimes committed by the ABiH, brutal crimes committed by the ABiH 3rd Corps soldiers, soldiers subordinated to both accused. ABiH 3rd Corps troops also committed crimes in the bigger towns, in the bigger towns in Bugojno, in the municipality of Kakanj, in Vares. As you can see on the map, it's in the eastern areas of the 3rd Corps area of command. And also, and in particular, in Zenica. In Zenica, the location of the two accused's headquarters, literally under their own eyes. Your Honours, I will now detail the executions and massacres committed by the subordinates of the two accused. We will show you a further map. It shows the locations where the crimes were committed. You have Dusina in the south of Zenica and you have, as already mentioned, Miletici to the north-west of Zenica, as Maline and Bikosi. From this map, Your Honours, you can also see the distances from the crime scenes to Zenica, to Zenica, the town where both accused were based. And the distances were small distances; 11 kilometres between Zenica and Dusina, 15 kilometres between Zenica and Miletici; and not much more, 16 kilometres, between Maline and Bikosi. The first crime, the first crime, Your Honours, concerns the execution of a Bosnian Serb civilian and five surrendered HVO soldiers on 26 January 1993 in Dusina and the killing of a further surrendered HVO soldier on the very same day in the same area. For the ease of reference and for better understanding, we will now show you the first two photographs. The first photograph, Your Honours, shows the hamlet, the few houses of which the hamlet of Dusina is comprised. At the lower side of this photograph, you see a house, a white house, some sort of a white house with a garage. In the front of this house -- in front of this house the victims were murdered. What happened? ABiH 3rd Corps troops, subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic, lined up eight men on the road and shot six of the eight. In the early morning hours of 26 January 1993, acting on orders of the accused Hadzihasanovic, 3rd Corps soldiers attacked a number of villagers in the Lasva Valley area, including Dusina. HVO soldiers, under the command of the local HVO commander, Zvonko Rajic, soon surrendered to the attacking 3rd Corps forces. They were detained for a while. At about 1500 hours, 3.00 p.m. in the afternoon the same day, hours after their surrender, 3rd Corps soldiers ordered eight -- eight of them out and lined them up on the road in spot of the house with the garage. The next photograph, which is already on the screen, Your Honours, shows you the spot of the execution. 3rd Corps soldiers then shot six -- six of the eight, one by one murdering Vojislav Stanisic, Niko Kegelj, Stipo Kegelj, Vinko Kegelj, Pero Ljubicic, and Augustin Rados. Your Honours, you will hear one of the two survivors. His testimony will describe the details of the crime, details which leave you with no other -- no other conclusions that these murders can only be described as an execution, brutal, brutal, and cynical. These were not the only murders, not the only murders of subordinates of the accused Hadzihasanovic on that day. The evidence, Your Honours, will also show that Sheriff Petkovic, Sheriff Petkovic, the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade 2nd Battalion and as such subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic killed the surrendered local HVO commander, Zvonko Rajic, by firing several shots with an automatic weapon from close range, from very close range. You will hear witnesses, Your Honours -- you will hear witnesses in this courtroom describing the terrible circumstances of this murder, a further murder at least as brutal and cynical as the execution of the six. The victims of the murders were brought to the morgue in Zenica. We will now show a number of stills from a video - there are nine stills - showing the victims of the murders and showing the terrible wounds, the terrible gunshot wounds and other wounds inflicted by the subordinates of the accused. The photographs show the six killed: Vojislav Stanisic, Niko Kegelj, Stipo Kegelj, Pero Ljubicic, and Augustin Rados. And Your Honours, you can see on a number of such photographs the gunshot wounds which caused the death of the accused. The second crime, Your Honours, the second crime concerns killing, the killing of four surrendered HVO soldiers on 29 April 1993 in Miletici. Between the evening hours of 24 April 1993 and the morning hours of the following day, 3rd Corps soldiers subordinated to both accused singled out four captured HVO soldiers, first mutilated, and then brutally murdered four of them. Again, for illustration we will show a few photographs; first, an aerial photograph showing the village of Miletici. On 24 April 1993, during evening hours, soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade arrived in that village in Miletici. They found the villagers gathering in two houses, gathering for protection. From one of the houses, an HVO soldier shot one 3rd Corps soldier. Consequently, the subordinates of the accused attacked the house, took the villagers out, and tied their hands and walked them to the village of Mehurici, some 2 kilometres away from Miletici. The 3rd Corps soldiers selected four Croat men from this group, from the group, namely Franjo Pavlovic, Tihomir Pavlovic, Vlado Pavlovic, and Anto Petrovic, and they kept them behind. You will hear villagers, Your Honours, villagers who came back during the night and in the early morning hours of the next morning. They will describe the horrible scene, the horrible scene they were confronted with. They found the four Croats -- young Croats murdered in one of the houses, murdered by the subordinates of the accused, both accused; not only murdered but obviously mutilated. The bodies displayed wounds to the heart and throat. The photograph which you have on your screen, Your Honours, shows the house where the victims were murdered. The following photograph shows the house where the victims were found. And the following photographs show the four victims. And again, you can see the wounds of the murdered four young Croats, Franjo Pavlovic, Tihomir Pavlovic, Vlado Pavlovic and Anto Petrovic. The third crime of murder concerns a massacre of about 30 Bosnian Croats, both civilians and surrendered HVO soldiers, on 08/02/1993 in the vicinity of the hamlet of Bikosi, close to the village of Maline. On 08/02/1993, 3rd Corps soldiers attacked Maline. After the surrender of the villagers and the defending HVO soldiers, they made them, the 3rd Corps soldiers, made them -- several hundred Bosnian Croats -- march to Mehurici. On the way, 3rd Corps soldiers selected a smaller group and directed them towards Bikosi. Soon they were joined by another group of wounded Croats. Under the escort of 3rd Corps soldiers, this new group continued walking, continued moving towards Mehurici. Near the hamlet of Bikosi, one of the prisoners started screaming. 3rd Corps soldiers -- again, 3rd Corps soldiers, subordinated to both accused - Hadzihasanovic and Kubura - then shot -- shot at the group with automatic rifles at close range, executing at least 24 Croat civilians and soldiers. The names are listed in the indictment. Four victims, Your Honours, managed to escape -- managed to escape after they had been seriously wounded. Their wounding amounts to cruel treatment as a violation of the laws and customs of war. The next photograph, Your Honours, shows the site of the massacre which is on the left side of the road in the photograph. Your Honours, subordinates to the both accused committed further crimes, and I'm now turning to the crimes committed by them in detention facilities. The ABiH 3rd Corps, throughout the indictment period, operated a large number of detention facilities within its area of responsibility. There were smaller ones, smaller ones and bigger ones dispersed over the area of the 3rd Corps. It was not a huge area at the time; it was a rather small area. The next map, Your Honours, details the locations of the 12 detention facilities where the crimes charged in the indictment have been committed. The map shows Bugojno in the very west, where six out of the 12 detention facilities were located; then we have Kakanj in the south-east of Zenica, the headquarters of the two accused; and then we have the area between Travnik and Zenica, again the area I already addressed; it's Mehurici, it's Orasac, and that there were detention facilities in the municipality of Travnik and there was a detention facility in Zenica. The distances are also shown on this map. And again, Your Honours, the distances were very small. We are talking about a range between 13 kilometres and 40 kilometres, most of them between 13 kilometres and about 20 kilometres. And in respect to the detention facility in Zenica, namely the Zenica Music School, Your Honours, the crimes were committed close to the front gates of the headquarters of the -- of the commanders of the perpetrators; namely, the two accused. In Zenica, Your Honours, the ABiH 3rd Corps 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was using the Zenica Music School, not far away from the 7th Muslim Brigade's headquarters and situated very close, very close to the 3rd Corps headquarters as its military police headquarters. The next map, Your Honours, we prepared to assist you, will show that the Zenica Music School was only 1 kilometre separated between General Hadzihasanovic's 3rd Corps headquarters, and it will also show that the headquarters of the accused Kubura was only about 2 kilometres away from the Zenica Music School -- music school. The Zenica Music School itself, Your Honours, we will show on the next two photographs. The first photographs show the Zenica Music School, the building of the Zenica Music School. It shows it from outside obviously. It's a building, Your Honours -- the Zenica Music School is a building situated in one of the main streets in Zenica -- of Zenica, right in the heart of the town. The second photograph, Your Honours, shows the cell, the cell in the Zenica Music School, the room in which the detainees were imprisoned, some of them for days; others for weeks, if not months. The living conditions in the Zenica Music School were poor. They were very poor. Up to 50 prisoners had to use a bucket as their toilet and they were not allowed to wash themselves. The food the detainees were provided with were starvation rations. Your Honours, you will hear a victim testifying in this courtroom, testifying that he lost 22 kilograms in 50 days, and you will hear another victim testifying that he lost 31 kilograms within 58 days. But worse, Your Honours, much worse is that in this building, the Zenica Music School, in this room you've seen just now and in other rooms of the very same building subordinates to both accused systematically -- systematically abused prisoners by regular and brutally beating them with a wide variety of weaponry. The implements of their brutality included rifle butts, wooden sticks and handles, truncheons, knuckle-dusters, staves, boots, and telephone cables. The beatings, Your Honours, the beatings were daily. They were daily and brutal. You will hear victims, former detainees, testifying that every night, literally every night, the guards took out prisoners for what they called singing lessons. Singing lessons, a very cynical description of what was nothing else but brutal beatings. The sounds of the beatings and the distressed cries for help could be heard in the centre of Zenica each and every night. You will hear a victim describing how he was beaten with sticks, chair legs, and truncheons for several hours before being locked in a small courtroom crammed with 48 other prisoners. Another victim, Your Honours, will detail how he was hit with rubber truncheons while his hands were handcuffed behind his back. And you will hear yet another victim telling how he was beaten with shovel handles and kicked on the chest until he lost consciousness. You will hear another one detailing how he was beaten with truncheons, wooden handles, and knuckle-dusters until he was unconscious. He was then ordered to catch the blood that was dripping off his head and threatened with death if any blood fell on the floor. And, Your Honours, you will hear a victim describing being beaten on his face, the shoulders, and the back of his head with police rubber sticks. When he begged for water, the guard took him to the communal tap. While trying to drink, the guard struck his head on the back and the witness hit his face on the tap and cut his face under his left eye and nose. As he lost consciousness, the guards poured water over him and kicked him while he was laying on the floor. The ongoing -- the ongoing and systematic mistreatment of prisoners in the Zenica Music School made it inevitable that at least one would succumb to his injuries. The victim was Jozo Maracic, a wounded HVO soldier. On 08/02/1993 he died after repeated severe beatings by subordinates of the two accused. On that day, in the early morning hours or in the early evening, guards took him out of the basement, the room that we showed you on the photograph. The remaining prisoners heard the terrible sounds of another brutal beating. When the guards brought him back, he was no longer breathing. He was dead. The Zenica Music School, Your Honours, was not the only detention facility in which subordinates of the two accused mistreated -- systematically mistreated detainees. There were many more. Several were in the municipality of Travnik. In the municipality of Travnik, the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade used the former JNA barracks. The 306th Brigade use both the Mehurici Elementary School and the blacksmith shop. Mujahedin -- Mujahedin within the ABiH 3rd Corps Group Bosanska Krajina used the Orasac camp in Orasac. Again, we prepared a number of photographs to assist Your Honours. The first photograph will show the former JNA barracks in Travnik. This is obviously a huge military barracks located in the town of Travnik, used as headquarters for the 3rd Corps operational group, the OG Bosanska Krajina. Several of its cells are shown on the next photograph, Your Honours. Small cells - you can see the entrance door to one of the cells right now, small cells, and you will see on the next photograph a sample of such a cell -- small cells, close, as witnesses will testify, to the office -- to the office of Mehmed Alagic, the OG commander at the time subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic. In and outside these cells, subordinates to the accused Hadzihasanovic, beat detainees, beat them systematically and on a regular basis. They were beaten with shovel handles. They were beaten with pick axe handles. And they were beaten with wet knotted towels. You will hear, Your Honours, you will hear victims testifying that they were beaten to a point where they were immobile and unconscious. Another victim will tell you that he was forced to strip naked before being beaten with fists, police truncheons, a metal bar, and a chair until he passed out. In all, as in all detention facilities, Your Honours, detainees in the former JNA barracks were beaten upon their arrival. They were beaten during the day and they were beaten during the night. They were beaten during interrogation. They were beaten for many reasons. They were beaten to intimidate, and they were beaten to humiliate them. And sometimes they were beaten for no reason. And as in the Zenica Music School, the systematic and brutal beatings resulted in the death, the death of at least one prisoner. This time the victim was a young Bosnian Croat detainee, an unnamed victim of the systematic -- the systematic and brutal mistreatment by the subordinates of the accused Hadzihasanovic. He was beaten to death in May 1993. During the night, guards took the victim out for another brutal beating. They brought him back to the detention cell very badly beaten. Prisoners called the guards to attend to the prisoners; they didn't. The next morning - the next morning - the prisoner was dead. Not far from Travnik, Your Honours, in Mehurici, the ABiH 3rd Corps operated further detention facilities. One of them was the Mehurici Elementary School. The next photograph shows its gymnasium hall where the detainees were held. The detainees were several hundred Bosnian Croats from Maline, mostly civilians. They were detained in this detention facility. They were kept in cramped and overcrowded conditions with inadequate food and inadequate water. The washing and hygiene facilities were poor. The prisoners -- again, several hundred prisoners -- were allowed access to only one toilet. One pot of warm water between them had to suffice for a day, had to suffice to wash the babies and to dress the wounds. And detainees were given little food, very little food. You will hear a victim, a female, a female testifying that she weighed only 30 kilogrammes after her release. Beatings were also not unusual in the Mehurici Elementary School. You will hear victims testifying that men whom the guards considered HVO members were selected, were singled out for interrogation and beatings. Another detention facility the 3rd Corps operated in Mehurici was the blacksmith shop, only a few hundred metres away from the Mehurici Elementary School. The next photograph shows you the blacksmith shop from outside and inside and the photographs show you the cramped conditions of confinement. The photograph you have now on the screen, Your Honours, shows the blacksmith shop from outside, and the next photograph gives you a very good impression of the cramped conditions inside. You will hear victims describing -- describing that subordinates to the accused Hadzihasanovic kept up to 13, 13 prisoners in the three windowless garages measuring around 3 square metres. You will hear victims who will tell that they had to sleep on the concrete floor and that they were given a small plastic bucket to use as a toilet. But worse, as in all other detention facilities, beatings, brutal beatings, mostly with wooden sticks, were the daily routine, the daily routine. A witness will describe, Your Honours, how a soldier entered the garage, kicked him in the face, which resulted in him losing several teeth. The next two photographs, Your Honours, will show you -- the first one, the area; and then the second one, the building of the Orasac camp. The photograph which is now on your screen, Your Honours, shows the area of Orasac, the little hamlet in the background, and the two houses in the front: You have the white house on the more left-hand side, and this, Your Honours, was the Orasac camp. The Orasac camp was run by Mujahedin, Mujahedin who were known -- who were very, very well known for their brutality. And they were brutal. In October 1993, the Mujahedin regularly abducted Bosnian Croat civilians from Travnik, covered their bodies, bundled them into vehicles, and took them to Orasac, where they were beaten daily. They were beaten for hours. You will hear victims describing such systematic beatings. They will describe, Your Honours, that prisoners, when using the toilet, had to run a gauntlet of the soldiers, who hit them. You will hear yet another victim describing that a guard heated up a metal rod and made one prisoner to hold it, and you will hear further witnesses describing all sorts of further mistreatment, both physical and psychological. Not surprisingly, Your Honours, as in the Zenica Music School, as in the former JNA barracks in Travnik, the systematic brutality in the Orasac camp resulted in the death of at least one prisoner. This time, Your Honours, the death was not the result of a beating. This time the death of the victim was the result of a beheading, a beheading that can only -- that can only be described as a ritual beheading. You will hear witnesses -- witnesses who had to observe the terrible murder, who will detail that on 20th of October, 1993 Mujahedin -- Mujahedin subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic took Dragan Popovic, Dragan Popovic, a Bosnian Croat civilian, together with other prisoners out of his cell and lined them up in front of a freshly dug hole. A Mujahedin took Dragan Popovic to the other side of the hole and slit his throat. Another Mujahedin severed his head from the body. The commander of the Mujahedin made the other prisoners kiss -- made them kiss the forehead and the lips of Dragan Popovic's head after his beheading. Finally, Your Honours - finally - two prisoners were forced to bury the dead body in the prepared -- in the prepared grave. The municipality of Kakanj is another scene of crimes committed by 3rd Corps soldiers in 3rd Corps detention facilities. In Kakanj, the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, a unit subordinated to both accused, used the Motel Sretno. The Motel Sretno, as you will see on the next photograph, Your Honours, the Motel Sretno, is a prominent -- a very prominent building located between the highway and Zenica. We prepared for your assistance, Your Honours, two buildings showing the Motel Sretno from outside. In its basement there were a number of cells, small cells, in which the prisoners were confined. In the Motel Sretno, systematic, brutal, and daily beatings were the daily occurrence. You will hear again victims who will describe such beatings with batons, sticks, a metal hook and rifle butts. Another victim will describe, Your Honours, how the prisoners were forced to beat each other. You will hear a further victim telling how he was beaten with wooden broom handles until he was unconscious. When he woke up, soldiers were urinating on him. And you will hear a victim who was hit -- was hit on his right kidney with a police truncheon after telling the guards that he had kidney problems. This witness, after his release, had two displaced kidneys, six broken ribs, and a badly damaged vertebrae. ABiH soldiers -- ABiH 3rd Corps soldiers did not only run detention facilities in the municipalities of Zenica, Travnik, and Kakanj, they also established a number of detention facilities in the small town of Bugojno to confine hundreds - hundreds - of mainly Bosnian prisoners of war and civilians. In 1993, the ABiH 3rd Corps operational group, the OG Zapad military police and soldiers of the ABiH 3rd Corp OG Zapad 307th Brigade used the Gimnazija school building, the convent building, the Slavonija Furniture Salon, the FC Iskra Stadium, the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School, and the Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina building as temporary detention facilities. These six detention facilities were operated within a small area, a very small area. The next map, Your Honours, shows you the town of Bugojno, ask you can see, as marked on the map, that the detention facilities were very close to each other. They were sometimes only situated within an area of a few hundred metres. The 3rd Corps transferred its prisoners between its various detention facilities, moving them from the one detention facility to the next one. We will now show a few photographs showing the Gimnazija school building. The first photograph shows it from outside. The following three photographs show the cells -- the cells, the very small cells in its basement. There were three cells next to each other, all of the same size and all small, all very small. And the fifth photograph, Your Honours, shows you its gymnasium hall. The Gimnazija school building was a particularly brutal detention facility in which soldiers subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic detained both civilians and HVO soldiers. Your Honours, you've seen the three cells on the photographs. Each of the cells were extremely small. They were dark, and they were poorly ventilated and they contained no sanitation facilities. You will hear a victim, Your Honours, detailing that within days one of these cells was packed -- within one day, one of the cells was packed with some 45 Croat prisoners. These prisoners, as the others who arrived later, were also the object of systematic brutal beatings by the 3rd Corps guards. In the Gimnazija school building, the beatings were also part of the daily routine. Every night the guards took out prisoners outside and beat them. A victim will describe a particularly severe beating during which his hands were handcuffed behind his back, he was kicked to the feet and kidney and was beaten with an electric cable for an hour before losing consciousness. The same -- the same victim lost 50 kilogrammes in weight during his incarceration. Not only he, but other detainees suffered from the starvation rations of food, often some lentils in water and bread just once a day. Another form of cruel treatment, Your Honours, prisoners of the Gimnazija school building were also forced to give blood. Prisoners were taken outside, taken out for forced labour assignments, a very common feature of all detention facilities or most of the detention facilities in Bugojno. 3rd Corps soldiers who were doing so seriously endangered the lives of the detainees by forcing them to dig trenches at the front lines. Another detention facility forming part of the system of the 3rd Corps detention facilities in Bugojno was the convent building. We will first show you six photographs. These photographs, Your Honours, will show you the convent building. The one you have on the screen shows you the convent building, also known as the Marxist centre, from outside. Then you will see on the next photograph one of the cells from outside, and the next three photographs will illustrate the cramped conditions of the two cells in the inside of the convent building. Small cells in the basement of the building, two small cells; and the last photograph, Your Honours, the last photograph which we will show you in a few seconds, gives you an impression of the view the prisoners had from inside this detention facility. And you can see this detention facility was not somewhere; it was in the town of Bugojno itself. The prisoners of the convent building suffered mistreatment of a similar nature as those in the Gimnazija school building. Guards subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic kept the detainees in confined unsanitary conditions. They were not properly fed. And again, in a systematic manner, they beat the HVO prisoners. And as it was normal in all detention facilities in Bugojno, prisoners of the convent building were also taken out, taken out for forced labour. They were taken out daily to collect bodies at the front line and to dig graves. As in the Zenica Music School, as in the former JNA Travnik barracks, and as in the Orasac camp, Your Honours, a prisoner was murdered, murdered by the subordinates of the accused Hadzihasanovic. You will hear a victim -- a witness -- you will hear a witness testifying about the brutal murder of Mario Zrno. Mario Zrno, an HVO prisoner whilst taking out for forced labour assignments and weakened from the lack of food and the physical labour, he collapsed. 3rd Corps soldiers then beat him into unconsciousness. He was taken back to the convent building in Bugojno. The report of the Zenica MUP state security station listed Mario Zrno as a prisoner of war, beaten black and blue, and tortured -- and tortured until he died. Not far -- not far from the convent building, the 3rd Corps used the Slavonija Furniture Salon as another temporary detention centre. The next photograph shows you the Slavonija Furniture Salon from outside a building, a rather huge building in the town centre of Bugojno. And we have prepared another photograph that shows you its cell, its cell in the basement from inside. This room, Your Honours, this room you have in front of you on the screen was possibly -- was possibly the worst detention facility in Bugojno. 3rd Corps soldiers subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic kept the prisoners in its basement. It was small -- it was small, and it was dark, and it was covered with about 10 to 15 centimetres water on the floor. The daily beatings were brutal. They commenced on the first day after the arrival of the prisoners. They were called out -- they were called out one by one and beaten one after the other, and the beatings didn't stop until their release. You will hear a victim describing that he was made to lie on his stomach and beaten -- beaten simultaneously by four or five soldiers. He was kicked and he was hit with a rubber baton. He was tramped on his fingers with their boots. And you will hear the same witness -- the same victim detailing a beating with a metal pipe, a metal bar and a wooden bat for over half an hour, having a rifle placed next to his head with the threat of death. In the Slavonija Furniture Salon, detainees were also taken out for work assignments. They were taken out to dig graves. They were beaten on the way, and they were forced -- they were forced to beat each other. On one occasion, while digging graves, guards threw large rocks at the prisoners, smashing one prisoner in the head and injuring another. And again, also -- again, also in the Slavonija Furniture Salon, at least one prisoner died. He died as a result -- as the result of the brutal beatings by the accused Hadzihasanovic's subordinates. On 5 August 1993, the guards called the prisoner upstairs. The prisoners were brutally beaten, one at a time, by four or five soldiers with metal pipes, with bars, with wooden bats. One of the HVO prisoners, Your Honours, Mladen Havranek, did not survive the brutal beating. You will hear witnesses describing him having collapsed when he returned downstairs. He had been beaten into unconsciousness. He had no pulse. He was no longer breathing. Other prisoners took his body upstairs and left the body with the guards. The same document that detailed Mario Zrno's death describes Mladen Havranek as a prisoner for -- called out of a group of prisoners, beaten black and blue, and died in the arms of prisoners on the way to the hospital. There were other detention facilities in Bugojno. Another detention facility as large as it was notorious was the FC Iskra Stadium. The FC Iskra Stadium, a football stadium of a significant size, can be seen on the next sequence of photographs. The first two ones which will appear on your screens, Your Honours, now show the FC Iskra Stadium, a football stadium, at the south-east entrance of Bugojno from outside. And the following photographs show you its changing rooms, the changing- rooms of the FC Iskra Stadium football stadium from inside, and you can see that these changing rooms, which were the actual cells of the detention facility, were small ones. The FC Iskra Stadium was a well-known detention facility. Several hundred of Croat HVO detainees went through it, but also a number of Bosnian Croat civilians, and amongst the detainees there were also Serbs from Bugojno. 3rd Corps soldiers -- 3rd Corps guards, subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic, subjected the detainees in the FC Iskra Stadium to the same systematic cruel treatment as in the other detention facilities in Bugojno. The same systematic mistreatment means beatings, threats, and forced labour on the front lines digging trenches. You will hear victims, a representative sample, a sample only of the hundreds of detainees of the FC Iskra Stadium describing the systematic beatings. Your Honours have seen the photographs of the changing rooms. You will hear victims, former detainees, describing that more than 140 prisoners were detained in such small cells measuring about 11 to 6 metres. Another witness will tell you that about 300 prisoners were crammed into two changing rooms, a small hall, and a hallway. And you will hear former detainees detailing the little food they received, very little; 13 pieces of bread and 20 litres of watery soup for 300 detainees every day and for weeks. There are further photographs, Your Honours, we have prepared; the next two ones show you the Vojin Paleksic elementary school. The first one shows it from the outside, and the second one shows the gymnasium hall where the prisoners -- the detainees were held. The Vojin Paleksic elementary school was just another prison forming part of the 3rd Corps system of detainees in Bugojno. The very same -- the very same systematic pattern of mistreatment of detainees was repeated in this detention facility. Subordinates to the accused Hadzihasanovic crammed about 300 prisoners into the gymnasium hall, which was about the size of a basketball court. Detainees were beaten, they were beaten brutally, and they were beaten regularly. They were beaten with truncheons. You will hear a victim describing such a beaten by six soldiers resulting in the unconsciousness of the detainee, and as it was typical for the detention facilities in Bugojno, prisoners, detainees from the Vojin Paleksic elementary school were also taken out for work digging trenches on the front side -- on the front side against the Serbs, thus exposing them to constant enemy fire. The last two photographs, Your Honours, illustrate the Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina building. Again, first a view from outside; the second photograph, showing a cell from its inside gives an impression, gives a pretty good impression of the conditions in this detention facility. As in the Slavonija Furniture Salon, also in the Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina building the floor was covered with water, several centimetres of water. Bosnian Croat prisoners were packed into the few small cells. You will hear a victim, Your Honours, describing how four prisoners were detained in such a cell, measuring about 1.5 to 2 metres in size. In the Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina building, subordinates to the accused Enver Hadzihasanovic also systematically beat and mistreated the prisoners. You will hear a victim detailing the brutal beatings, brutal to the extent that some of the prisoners lost consciousness. These are the underlying crimes, Your Honours, for Counts 3 and 4 of the indictment, murders and cruel treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, subordinates of the two accused did not only commit the crimes I was detailing before this break; subordinates of the two accused committed further crimes. In the course of -- after having finished their combat activities, ABiH 3rd Corps soldiers repeatedly -- repeatedly either plundered or plundered and destroyed without any military justification Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Serb homes, buildings, and personal property. Throughout the indictment period, 3rd Corps soldiers subordinated to the accused plundered and destroyed such property and they regularly plundered and destroyed it. This occurred in different geographical areas of the 3rd Corps. 3rd Corps attacks were frequently followed by the rampant looting and burning of Croat and Serb civilian property. It became a common feature -- a very common feature following attacks of 3rd Corps troops. The next map, Your Honours, we will show shows you the respective areas. Again -- again, as can be seen from the map, the accuseds' subordinates plundered and burnt down houses not somewhere far away but close to the own -- their own headquarters, that is, virtually under their own eyes. Subordinates to both accused during and/or after the attack on Miletici broke into houses of villagers and stole their belongings and livestock. During the series of heavy attacks of ABiH 3rd Corps troops in June 1993 in Central Bosnia, they plundered and burnt down houses in Guca Gora, in Maline, in Cukle, in the municipality of Travnik, and in the area of Susanj, Ovnak, Brajkovici, and Grahovcici. As you can see on the map, Your Honours, the latter ones form part of the municipality of Zenica. The Prosecution witnesses, villagers, and 3rd Corps soldiers alike will testify that 3rd Corps soldiers treated as their own personal property cars, trucks, tractors, furniture, kitchen equipment, televisions, video recorders, radio, fridges, stuffs, and washing machines belonging to the residents forced to flee the fighting. In Cukle, soldiers were even instructed by a loudspeaker to get everything out -- to get everything out before burning the houses in the village. And in the very same village, soldiers subordinated to the accused forced -- forced the villagers to give away their valuables and money. The most brazen looting, plundering, and burning occurred -- occurred before the eyes of the Swedish peacekeepers in Vares in November 1993. After soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, subordinates to the accused Kubura, had participated in taking Vares from HVO control, they walked through the streets firing at windows and smashing cars. In this wild rampage, which was also witnessed by the international media, they looted and burnt houses, including the town's buildings and businesses. They took cars -- buses -- cars, buses, and trucks of food, leaving behind a devastated -- a devastated town. 3rd Corps soldiers also didn't spare the religious sites protected as cultural and religious monuments by the Geneva Conventions. During the early June 1993 attacks, 3rd Corps soldiers seriously - seriously - damaged both the monastery in Guca Gora and the church of St. John the Baptist in Travnik. In Guca Gora, a prominent -- a very prominent symbol of the Catholic faith in Central Bosnia, subordinates of the accused Hadzihasanovic smeared feces on the walls and pews, broke stained glass windows, graffitised the walls and tried to smash a large fresco of the wall behind the altar. Subordinates of the accused Hadzihasanovic also damaged the church of St. John the Baptist in Travnik by vandalising sculptures, paintings and their organ, and damaging the windows. As in Guca Gora, walls were covered with graffiti; stalls and frescos were smeared with paint. Your Honours, these are the crimes that form the basis for the indictment. Subordinates of the accused, not the accused themselves, committed the crimes. Both accused are, however -- they are, however, criminally liable under Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute, command responsibility, because they did not prevent these crimes from being committed and they did not punish the perpetrators of these crimes. A number of issues will arise during trial. Crucial -- crucial will be those related to criminal liability under Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. In that respect, Your Honours, the Prosecution will prove that a superior-subordinate relationship existed between the accused and the alleged criminal perpetrators. The Prosecution will prove that the accused knew or had reason to know that the perpetrators were about to commit the criminal acts, or had done so; in plain language, that the accused were put on notice of such crimes. And the Prosecution will also prove - and this will go to the very heart of this case - that the accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal acts or to punish the perpetrators. Your Honours, the accused, General Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Amir Kubura, they were the superiors of the alleged perpetrators. The two accused had effective control over their subordinates committing the crimes. Both accused had the material ability to prevent offences or to punish the criminal -- the principal offenders. The two accused -- both accused demonstrated de jure and de facto authority. General Hadzihasanovic, from 14 November 1992, commanded the ABiH 3rd Corps. He remained in this position until he was appointed chief of the Supreme Command staff of the ABiH on 1st of November, 1993. As the 3rd Corps Commander, he had subordinated to him a number of OGs - operative groups - brigades, and other units. These units included the units, Your Honours, whose members committed the crimes as detailed in the indictment; namely, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, the 303rd Mountain Brigade, the 306th Mountain Brigade, the 314th Mountain Brigade, the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade, the 307th Brigade, and the Military Police of the Operative Group Zapad. The accused Hadzihasanovic was both their de jure and de facto commander. Numerous orders issued by the accused Hadzihasanovic to his subordinates, who committed the crimes alleged, and the implementation and reporting back demonstrates the control he exercised. These documents will show, Your Honours, that the accused Hadzihasanovic did everything -- he did everything what a military commander in his position as a corps commander was required to do. We will show that the accused Hadzihasanovic decided on the organisational structures of the 3rd Corps, including the formation of operative groups, the OGs, the subordinate units under such OGs, and the appointment, promotion, and relief of subordinate commanders. We will also tender into evidence many orders, instructions, and directives of the accused Hadzihasanovic deploying troops and planning the preparation -- the preparation and implementing of military operations. Colonel Kubura -- Colonel Kubura became the acting commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade on 1st April 1993, from when he assumed de jure and de facto control of this brigade. On 21st July 1993 he was appointed the brigade's commander, a position he held until 16 March 1994 when he was assigned command of the 1st Corps, 1st Muslim Mountain Brigade. We will present -- the Prosecution will present military documents, ABiH documents of the same nature as those related to the accused Hadzihasanovic that will prove the accused Kubura de jure and de facto authority. Like General Hadzihasanovic, Colonel Kubura issued orders, instructions, and directives preparing for armed combat in the field, planning and conducting military operations, transmitting decisions of superior to subordinate commands, and controlling their implementation. I am now going to address Your Honours a specific aspect in respect to the subordination. I'm going to address the issue of the subordination of the Mujahedin. Who were the Mujahedin? The Mujahedin are foreign Muslim fighters, foreign Muslim fighters principally from Islamic countries. They subordinated to the 3rd Corps command and also deployed within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, committed numerous crimes, numerous crimes against the civilian population and prisoners of war throughout the indictment period and including crimes that form part of this indictment. We will present evidence, both witness testimony and documents, showing - showing - that the Mujahedin upon their arrival from mid-1992 onwards were used by the 3rd Corps command to assist 3rd Corps units in attacks on the enemy and, in particular, to lead such attacks and to undertake the more difficult military combat operations. Your Honours, you will hear witnesses -- you will hear witnesses in this courtroom describing the Mujahedin as shock troops. Other witnesses, witnesses from within the 3rd Corps, will demonstrate that they were used to spearhead military operations, military operations of the 3rd Corps. The Prosecution's evidence will also show that the Mujahedin were in particular involved in combat operations conducted by the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Finally, on 13th August of 1993, after the accused Hadzihasanovic had requested the ABiH Supreme Command to do so, the Mujahedin within the 3rd Corps area were deployed in a separate detachment -- a separate detachment called El Mujahed directly subordinated to him. The Prosecution's evidence will prove that the Mujahedin upon their arrival were incorporated into the 3rd Corps military structure, including the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. The evidence we will present will prove that both accused, General Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Amir Kubura, both accused exercised effective control over the Mujahedin, both accused had the material ability to prevent offences and/or to punish crimes that Mujahedin committed. Your Honour, both accused knew or they had reason to know that the perpetrators were about to commit the crimes or had done so. We will present evidence, again both witness testimony and documentary evidence, that proves that the accused, both accused, had actual knowledge in respect to a substantial number of the crimes alleged in the indictment. In particular, the accused had actual knowledge about the murders, the execution, and the massacres. The murders were common public knowledge within a few days after they were committed. They were known in detail -- they were known in detail, including the fact that the subordinates to the accused had committed them and, without doubt - without doubt - the accused got to know about them. The Prosecution's evidence will show that the accuseds on numerous occasions were informed by the HVO, they were informed by ECMM representatives, and they were informed by UNPROFOR. In addition, they were informed by their own superiors, their own superiors requesting information. Documents such as orders of the accused and their reports up the chain of command will reveal - will reveal - their actual knowledge. More concrete, in respect to the execution in Dusina, the accused Hadzihasanovic very shortly after the incident - and we are talking about hours; we are talking about hours only - had direct knowledge of allegations of serious criminality against soldiers subordinated to him. We will tender -- we will tender into evidence a press release, a 3rd Corps press release, stating that Zvonko Rajic - now a quote - "A well-known extremist and six of his most loyal soldiers were killed in this conflict." We will tender into evidence a report of the accused Hadzihasanovic dated 27th of January, 1993, the day after the attack, reporting to the ABiH Supreme Command about a meeting on 26 January 1993, the day of the murders, between his deputy - Hadzihasanovic's deputy, Dzemo Merdan - Colonel Blaskic, the HVO operational SO and Central Bosnian commander; and UNPROFOR in which Colonel Blaskic had proposed -- had a proposed breaking of negotiations because of the death of seven HVO members. And we will tender into evidence another report of the accused Hadzihasanovic to the ABiH Supreme Command on allegations aired on the Croatian radio and television stating - and that's now a quote - "We checked all lies spread by the HTV about the alleged massacres of the Croatian population, as well as the lie about the alleged killings of seven unarmed HVO soldiers." Your Honours, what does this mean? That means that the accused Hadzihasanovic knew, he knew that on 26 January 1993 his subordinates had captured HVO soldiers. He knew that six or seven HVO soldiers, including the local HVO commander, were killed in Dusina on that day. And he knew that the Croats were alleging the ABiH had killed them after their surrender. The accused Hadzihasanovic had also direct knowledge of the murders in Miletici. We will present evidence that the day after the execution on 25th April 1993, Merdan, the accused Hadzihasanovic's deputy, and an ECMM officer travelled to Miletici to investigate - to investigate - the reports of a massacre. Following this visit, the ECMM wrote a report confirming the torture and the murder of four Croat victims. Another document, Your Honours, another document will prove that on 6 May 1993, the 306 Mountain Brigade reported to the 3rd Corps command organ for morale, information, propaganda, and religious matters about Miletici, stating that in response to the wounding of an Arab, the Mujahedin - the Mujahedin - had killed five Croat citizens. And a day later, on 7th May 1993, the HVO Central Bosnia information office wrote to ECMM, to ICRC, to UNPROFOR, and to the 3rd Corps command providing specific information, specific information about the murders in Miletici. The murders in Miletici also achieved international publicity. On 15th May 1993, the United Nations special rapporteur reported to the Security Council. He reported to the Security Council the following: "Field staff visited the village of Miletici north of Vitez and gathered testimony, testimony which alleges how on around 16th April members of government forces from neighbouring villages and Mujahedin encircled the village and selected five young Croat men. Some of them then tortured before they were executed." We will use this to prove that the accused Hadzihasanovic, within a short period of time - within a short period of time - had received from several sources detailed information that his subordinates had murdered the surrendered HVO soldiers. In respect to the accused's Kubura, Your Honours, we will show a series of documents, ABiH documents that will demonstrate that he, prior to the murders in Miletici, was well aware of the criminal conduct of his subordinate soldiers. It was the accused Kubura himself who on 8 April 1993 and following a complaint from the command of the 306 Mountain Brigade reported about the, what he describes, "unacceptable behaviour of some brigade members." Turning to the massacre in Maline and Bikosi and the direct knowledge the accused had about this massacre. The massacre in Maline and Bikosi, not at all a small event in Central Bosnia, taking into account that 24 Croats were killed, it was not a small event and it was not a small event in the area of the 3rd Corps. Accordingly, it was publicly known shortly - shortly - after it was committed. And not surprisingly it became known -- became also known to the ABiH Supreme Command Staff. Your Honours, we will present evidence, evidence that on 20th June 1993, following up the respective information, the ABiH deputy commander, Siba [phoen], visited the accused Hadzihasanovic in Zenica and asked him, asked him whether he knew about the execution of 35 people in Bikosi. The Defence are not contesting that on 9th August 1993 the accused Hadzihasanovic's deputy, Dzemo Merdan, together with an ECMM representative, visited Bikosi examining three grave sites. Dzemo Merdan, as the accused Hadzihasanovic's deputy, could not have participated without the accused Hadzihasanovic's knowledge. Like the Miletici murders, the massacre in Maline/Bikosi also attracted international attention. Following inquiries by the United Nations special rapporteur, the ABiH Supreme Command Delic, on behalf of the president of the Presidency, Izetbegovic, wrote a letter -- wrote a letter to the accused Hadzihasanovic requesting information about an alleged massacre in Maline on 8 July 1993. All this, Your Honours, all this provided specific notice to the accused Hadzihasanovic of the crimes alleged. Also the accused Kubura was on notice of his subordinates' actions. We will tender -- the Prosecution will tender a document into evidence that shows that on 20 June 1993 the accused Kubura issued an order to his subordinate commanders to prevent negative occurrences. Moreover, this order continues ordering the accused Kubura's subordinates to treat prisoners of war, especially the wounded, in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions. This order, issued only -- only several days after the massacre, seen together with the public knowledge of the crime as detailed, leads to the only -- the only available inference that the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 387 to 390. accused Hadzihasanovic, like the accused -- the accused Kubura, sorry -- the accused Kubura, like the accused Hadzihasanovic, had positive knowledge about the massacre. Both accused in many instances also knew about their subordinates' crimes committed in the detention facilities. Some of the detention facilities - for example, the Zenica Music School and the FC Iskra Stadium in Bugojno, were particularly notorious: Notorious in the sense that the detainees were subjected to inhumane treatment, notorious in the sense the detainees were brutally beaten, and notorious in the sense that superiors of the accused expressed their concern towards the accused and ordered them to ensure -- to ensure the prisoners are treated in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. The mistreatment of prisoners held at the Zenica Music School was particularly notorious in the sense that it was the subject of many -- many complaints, not only of international organisations such as the ECMM and the ICRC but also to the 3rd Corps command, complaints to the 3rd Corps command and the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. We will present a report showing that on 7th May 1993 the HVO information office informed -- informed the 3rd Corps command of the extreme maltreatment subjected on prisoners held in the Zenica Music School. Another document will show that the accused Hadzihasanovic met -- met with ECMM representatives on the same day in order to discuss the situation in the Zenica Music School. And we will present a witness, at the time a judge of the Zenica district military court and currently appointed to the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who on 13 June 1993 informed the accused Hadzihasanovic about complaints about mistreatment and beating of prisoners. The accused Hadzihasanovic replied. He replied to the effect that he had heard of it but had checked it and, as he said, "And it was okay." It wasn't okay, Your Honours; it wasn't okay at all. Five days after that meeting, Jozo Maracic died. He died after being beaten to death by the subordinates of the accused Hadzihasanovic. He was killed just 1 kilometre away from the accused Hadzihasanovic's headquarters. He was killed just 2 kilometres away from the accused Kubura's headquarters, murdered by the accused Kubura's direct subordinates. The accused Kubura did not have only actual knowledge of the mistreatment of prisoners in the Zenica Music School; he also knew about the brutal beatings in the Motel Sretno. He knew about it because a victim told him. You will hear, Your Honours, you will hear this former detainee. This detainee will describe -- will describe how he, after his release, was taken by HVO soldiers to a meeting between the HVO and the ABiH, monitored by UNPROFOR. The accused Kubura was the senior ABiH representative at this meeting. At this meeting, the victim informed the participants, including the accused Kubura, about the injuries inflicted on him by 3rd Corps guards at the Motel Sretno. These injuries were six broken ribs, a badly damaged vertebrae, and two displaced kidneys, caused by brutal beatings with a police truncheon. The accused Hadzihasanovic also had positive knowledge, positive knowledge of the crimes committed by his subordinates in the Motel Sretno. He, the accused Hadzihasanovic, at the time lived in Kakanj. He lived in Kakanj only several hundred metres away from the Motel Sretno. He lived there knowing about the cruel treatment, knowing about the cruel treatment because he was informed about it. We will tender documents into evidence that show that he was informed by the HVO about the maltreatment of prisoners in Kakanj, in Kakanj in the Motel Sretno. This knowledge came from at least -- from at least two sources: First, on 21st May 1993, by way of a protest letter; and again, on 21st June 1993, on the occasion of a meeting at BritBat headquarters. In respect to other detention facilities, the accused Hadzihasanovic was provided with inquiry notice. He was provided with information to the extent necessary to require further information. The detention facilities in the municipalities of Travnik and Bugojno formed part of the organised structure of detention facilities within the area of the 3rd Corps. Prisoners were moved from one detention facility to the other, in some instances crossing borders of municipalities and areas of responsibility of military units. Such organised movements required planning. They required logistics, and they required manpower. And they required approval, approval by the accused Hadzihasanovic. Finally, as can be seen from the map, the distances -- the map that will show up at your screen right now -- the distances between the detention facilities and the accused Hadzihasanovic's headquarters were small; in several instances, less than 20 kilometres. The accused knew his area of responsibility and he knew it very well. Quite often he was in the field visiting -- visiting the areas where the detention facilities were located. People used to talk about the crimes, both the civilians and soldiers on both sides, and the accused Hadzihasanovic talked to people. The accused Hadzihasanovic positively knew about the cruel treatment of detainees in the Zenica Music School. He positively knew about the cruel treatment of detainees in the Motel Sretno. He positively knew about the existence of the other detention facilities. Being aware -- being aware of the crimes in the Zenica Music School and the Motel Sretno, he had reason to know -- the accused Hadzihasanovic had reason to know about the cruel treatment in the other detention facilities. Your Honours, both accused also knew about the plunder, and they also knew about the wanton destruction. You will hear a witness, a command-staff member of a unit subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic, stating that looting by 3rd Corps members and the burning of Croat and Serb property was endemic, was endemic in the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility throughout the indictment period. It was common; plundering and destroying was common to the extent that the accused Hadzihasanovic, well aware of this, repeatedly ordered his subordinate commanders to prevent ABiH soldiers from stealing, looting, and burning property. We will present evidence detailing that he even knew which of his subordinates' units were - and that's a quote - "The most active in this illegal behaviour." And he knew about specific incidents, specific incidents of looting and destruction, such as in Guca Gora after the attack on 8 June 1993. A few days later -- a few days later, only on 16 June 1993, he sent an order -- he sent an order to the 306 Brigade command specifically referring to what had happened. The document we will tender into evidence, Your Honours, reads as follows: "During and after the combat activities in your zone of responsibility, large-scale looting and burning of facilities to Croatian population has occurred." Not only did the accused Hadzihasanovic know about this and other specific incidents of looting and burning down of houses. The accused Kubura knew about such incidents as well. We will present a document, an order of the accused Kubura to his subordinates of 20 June 1993, stating that there have been incidents of illegal arrest of civilians, looting of their property and houses. In particular, the accused Kubura had knowledge about the looting and the burning down of houses by his subordinates in Vares. A document we will tender into evidence is an order of the command of the 6th Corps OG Visoko for November 1993 requesting to cease all unauthorised acts and withdrawal of the army saying that it was a personal order from the Supreme Commander to be implemented by the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was the accused Kubura. Accordingly, the accused Kubura on 5th November 1993 ordered all members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade out of Vares immediately and prohibited their staying there without his approval. But it goes further. A member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade who participated in the looting in Vares will testify. He will testify that there was no intervention by the 3rd Corps Commanders in regards to this looting because they had helped themselves to the war booty. Destruction and willful damage to institutions dedicated to religion were committed by the subordinates of the accused Hadzihasanovic. He had positive knowledge about the damage done to the monastery in Guca Gora. He had also positive knowledge about the damage to the church of St. John the Baptist in Travnik. Not without reason on 10 June 1993, two days after the main ABiH attack on Guca Gora, he issued an order stating, stating that the damaging and destroying religious sites was prohibited. This was not purely coincidental. One week later, on 17 June 1993, the accused attended -- the accused Hadzihasanovic attended a meeting with Stjepan Siber, the ABiH deputy commander, and Archbishop Puljic. You will hear, Your Honour, you will hear a witness describing that the archbishop informed him, informed the accused Hadzihasanovic that the interior of the Travnik church had been destroyed and that the accused Hadzihasanovic replied that he - and that's a quote - "had sensed trouble in the region." Your Honours, both accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal acts or to punish the perpetrators. What were the necessary reasonable measures both accused were required to take? The measures to take to prevent the crimes are stated in the Geneva Conventions and its additional Protocol I, well known at the time to the accused, both accused. Such measures include instructing the subordinate commanders and soldiers in their duties under international law; ordering that subordinates observe international humanitarian law and that any violation be punished; imposing sufficient discipline to enforce compliance with international humanitarian law; monitoring subordinate command areas and ensuring that all necessary measures to observe and implement international humanitarian law are taken; disciplining commanders who do not implement all necessary measures to observe and implement international humanitarian law, including the removal of such commanders from their posts. There are other measures, such as ordering that any violations of international humanitarian law by subordinates cease immediately, such as reporting the violation of -- violations of international law to superiors, initiating criminal prosecution of supervisors who cover breaches of international lw, and initiate criminal prosecution of subordinates who breach international humanitarian law. Your Honours, our military expert, the Prosecution's military expert witness, will show that both accused, General Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Kubura, could have taken such measures under the conditions at the time. The measures both accused were required to take to punish the crimes by their subordinates included immediately initiating an investigation to establish whether or not criminal breaches of international humanitarian law had in fact occurred and, if so, the circumstances of the crime, relevant witnesses, and other evidence, and the identity of the perpetrators. If the perpetrators had been identified, to detain the perpetrators and hand the perpetrators over to a competent authority; obtaining a report about the results of the investigation into the crime and any disciplinary measures taken by subordinate commanders. There are other measures, such as determining whether the seriousness of the crime requires disciplinary action or criminal prosecution. If the seriousness of the crime was granted, disciplinary action immediately takes steps to establish responsibility for breaches of discipline or pronounced disciplinary measures.
