And if the seriousness of the crimes were granted criminal prosecution to personally -- to personally and immediately initiate all measures necessary for the transfer of the case to the prosecuting agency and the initiation of criminal prosecution. The accused, both accused, could have taken these measures in accordance with a functional military disciplinary system which was established by the end of 1992. Its legal instruments included the order on enforcement of rules of military law in the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The legal instruments included the rules of operation for the military security service; they included the rules of service for the military police and the legal instruments available to the accused included the manual "Unmilitary Discipline". Regulations and decrees were enacted to establish three separate courts, each with defined jurisdiction; namely, the special military courts, the military disciplinary courts, and most relevant to this indictment, the district military courts. The 3rd Corps had a complete -- had a complete and functioning military prosecution system, a functioning prosecution military system throughout the indictment period. The accused Hadzihasanovic, as the corps commander, established a corps military disciplinary court in early 1993. He requested and he arranged the statutory appointment of its judges, its prosecutor, and its secretary. Many soldiers were disciplined in the 3rd Corps military disciplinary court throughout the indictment period. The 3rd Corps had a functioning legal department which advised the accused Hadzihasanovic on military and legal matters. District military courts and district military prosecutors' offices were also functioning throughout the indictment period. Judges and prosecutors of those courts will testify that the courts were functioning throughout the indictment period and, indeed, prosecuted many 3rd Corps soldiers for criminal offences. They will testify that the court needed a criminal report before it could investigate and prosecute crimes allegedly committed by 3rd Corps soldiers. And they will testify, Your Honours, that the courts investigated criminal offences committed by 3rd Corps soldiers when it received a criminal report from the 3rd Corps command and its units. However, they will testify that they did not prosecute any 3rd Corps soldiers for crimes classified as war crimes against the civilian population or prisoners of war. We will prove, Your Honours, that this system of criminal investigation and prosecution was working. It was working when the 3rd Corps command had chosen to utilise it. The accused made it work -- they made it work against HVO soldiers. The accused made it also work against ABiH soldiers if and when their subordinates' units' safety was jeopardised. And the accused made it even work in cases of minor disciplinary offences if and when the combat readiness of units under their command and control was jeopardised. The accused failed, however, they failed to make it work for the investigation and the punishment of any of the perpetrators who had committed the crimes as detailed in the indictment. The accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal acts or to punish the perpetrators. Your Honours, we will present evidence, evidence that allowed the military expert to draw the conclusion that both accused had the means available to comply with their legal duties. The accused had the means available to investigate. They had the means available to provide the district military-prosecutor officers with criminal -- criminal reports to enable them to prosecute the perpetrators. The accused Hadzihasanovic had the duty to order an investigation into allegations of criminality by his subordinates, as had the accused Kubura. They also had the means to do so. The 3rd Corps had a Military Police Battalion subordinated to the accused Hadzihasanovic's chief of staff, a military police battalion comprised of about 250 to 300 soldiers based nearby at the Zenica KP Dom. Every 3rd Corps brigade, including, of course, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, had its own military police. We will ask the Court to call a witness -- to call as a witness the 3rd Corps chief of security, the most senior person within the military security service in the 3rd Corps at the time. He will testify that every brigade commander had a duty under international and domestic law to have investigated criminal matters of which he had notice or reason to suspect that his subordinates had committed crimes. This included the duty to forward criminal reports to the district military prosecutor's offices. The corps commander could sign military reports to the district military court prosecutor. This witness, the then-3rd Corps chief of security, he will testify that he can't remember whether the accused Hadzihasanovic signed any criminal reports for referral to the district military prosecutor's offices. And this witness, Your Honours, he will also testify that he would have known had any brigade commanders been punished, demoted, or relieved of command for failing to punish or prevent the criminal activities of their subordinates. He does not know of any brigade commanders been punished, demoted, or relieved of their position for this reason while he was the chief of security. Like the accused Hadzihasanovic, the accused Kubura did not use the means available to him to investigate the crimes of his subordinates. And like the accused Hadzihasanovic, he did not use the military police assigned to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, the brigade under his command and effective control. Both accused failed to punish the crimes as detailed in the indictment. And in doing so and not using the other means as described earlier on, both accused also failed to prevent the crimes as detailed in the indictment. Your Honours, I will now briefly address the Prosecution's evidence. The Prosecution's case will be proven through the testimony of dozens of witnesses and, in addition, through several hundreds of documents. We will also tender further evidence such as photographs and video footage. The witnesses testifying about the crimes committed by the subordinates of the accused will be eyewitnesses to the killings, victims of the crimes committed in the detention facilities, and eyewitnesses to the other crimes detailed in the indictment. The witnesses testifying to the elements of the accuseds' command responsibility will mostly be international witnesses, such as the former ECMM and UNPROFOR members. The Prosecution will also call former military prosecutors, judges, and members of the 3rd Corps legal staff. We will call the former deputy commander of the ABiH, who told the accused Hadzihasanovic of the crimes of his subordinates, a number of so-called insider-type of witnesses, 3rd Corps soldiers, will complete the Prosecution's witness list. The documents the Prosecution will introduce as exhibits in their majority stem from the ABiH -- the ABiH main archive. Many of them are signed by the accused. In conclusion, the Prosecution evidence will prove the guilt of the accused, both accused. Your Honours, this concludes our opening statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the Prosecutor. Pursuant to Article 84 of the Rules of Evidence and procedure, the parties - the Defence, that is - can, if it so desire, make an opening statement. So I'm now going to ask the Defence of Mr. Hadzihasanovic whether they indeed do wish to make an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we've already informed you, the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic will be making its opening statement before it starts the Defence case, so that we shan't been making an opening statement today. I should also like to confirm that I consulted my client with regard to your question, and he stands by his position not to avail himself of the right provided to him under Rule 84. Thank you. -- 84 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. How about the Kubura Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Kubura take it is identical position as does the Hadzihasanovic Defence team with respect to an opening statement and also with respect to Mr. Kubura's statement, statement of the accused under Rule 84 bis; that is to say, the accused will not be making a statement today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So the Chamber takes note of this, that the parties will not be making opening statements at this juncture, and that the accused renounce their right under Rule 84 bis to make a statement themselves. That being the fact, we can go on to the presentation of evidence and the Prosecution case. The Prosecution will have a first witness, I believe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour; the Prosecution, however, suggests to have a break. Before the break, however, I wish to introduce and to take the opportunity to introduce the members of the trial team. Apart from myself, the Prosecution trial team consists of three experienced, very experienced lawyers: Mr. David Re, an attorney from Australia; Mr. Daryl Mundis, an attorney from the United States. And the Prosecution trial team will be completed within the next future -- within the near future by Mr. Chester Stamp, an experienced attorney from Jamaica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much to the Prosecution for introducing us to the Prosecution team. It's almost noon, so I think it would be preferable to adjourn, to take a short break, and from 11.55 to 12.25. So we're going to take up the proceedings with our first witness and going on to the end of the session without making any further breaks or adjournments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. We can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the accused if they can hear the simultaneous translation. Can you hear the simultaneous translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we shall start on the presentation of the Prosecution witnesses. It is now 12.30, and we are going to be having this hearing until quarter to 2.00. And the Prosecution can start its examination-in-chief until quarter to 2.00. We will then proceed with the cross-examination tomorrow, as this witness is going to be with us for two days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution does in fact anticipate that this witness will be here for two days. That's correct. The Prosecution calls Zeljko Cvijanovic. Mr. President, if I may, while the witness is being brought into the courtroom, and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, this witness will be testifying primarily with respect to the alleged murder of Zvonko Rajic in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you hear something? Could you give us your name, surname, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zeljko Cvijanovic. I was born on the 28th of July, 1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am living in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your current job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By occupation, I'm a driver. And currently I am disabled, so that I am 80 per cent invalid and I am not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So I would like to ask you to read the solemn declaration, which the usher is about to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may sit down. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecution so that they can proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that your current job is a driver, although you are disabled. Prior to the war, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The same. Before the war, I was a driver. I worked as a driver. I had a privately owned truck of my own, which still stands in front of my house, burnt down -- the remains of it, rather, were burnt when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, prior to the war in Central Bosnia, did you do compulsory service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when, where, and what your military duties encompassed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I served in the Yugoslav People's Army in Bitola. I was recruited as an infantry man, commander of an RBR detachment. After completing training, I worked in Bitola in the medical centre as head of the medical platoon, so in the same town in which I had been serving up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In what years did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell the Trial Chamber where you were living as of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in Lasva, where I was born, until we were captured and expelled from there, that is where I lived. This applies to me and my family.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We believe the witness said '87 instead of '77.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in what municipality or municipalities is the village of Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Lasva, where my house is and where I lived, belonged to Zenica municipality. However, this is at the meeting point. There are -- the meeting point between the municipalities of Kakanj, Zenica, and Busovaca. My house where I lived was actually in the territory of Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the conditions in the village of Lasva in 1992 with respect to the ethnicity of that town.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the Croats, there were about 56 family homes or households. As for Serbs, there were a little more. But the majority population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which ethnic group do you consider yourself a member of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: My father is a Serb, and my mother is a Croat, so I'd rather not declare myself to be either. I respect both my parents, and it is thanks to them that I am alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time during 1992 when ethnic tensions in Lasva intensified?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It became very tense. Initially it was the people of Serb ethnicity that were mistreated in Lasva, and they sought assistance from the Croats, and there were tensions immediately between the Croat and Muslim ethnicity and also in relation to the Serbs, because there were front lines already established where Serbs were waging war against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, in 1992 when you joined a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I was a military conscript, it was my duty by law that applied in the former Yugoslavia that I had to respond to the draft and fulfil my civil duties. I could choose at the time, because there was the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Croatian Defence Council. There were two legal armed forces, and you could opt for either of your own free will. Of course, I opted for the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council goes by the acronym HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate month in 1992 when you joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was around the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the interaction between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Lasva and the surrounding areas in 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the relationship between the BH army and the HVO at the time, at the beginning, appeared to be normal. There was heightened tension and the population was in fear in the evening. There were patrols consisting of two soldiers of the HVO and two soldiers of the Territorial Defence, as it was called in those days, but they were Muslim. So two Croats and two Muslims. And that is how it functioned at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that there was heightened tension and the population was in fear in the evening. What was the population afraid of at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I was saying, front lines already existed against the Serb side, so that the Serbs, the inhabitants who were Serbs, were mistreated, expelled, killed, beaten up, and of course those who survived the Golgotha came to seek aid and they addressed the commander at the time, Zvonko Rajic, who headed this platoon or the small number of us that were there, and normally this appeared as support of them, and that is when tensions increased, so that cooperation between the Croats and the Muslims became more and more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned Zvonko Rajic as being the head of a platoon. Can you tell us what unit Zvonko Rajic headed or was in command of.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Rajic headed a group of locals from Lasva. It was an independent unit. They had simply organised themselves, the inhabitants of Lasva, as they were in the minority, and he was mobilised to the HVO. The main command was in Busovaca. And Mr. Zvonko was in command of the militarily able-bodied men in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this unit that he commanded exclusively an HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively an HVO unit. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when fighting broke out in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when fighting broke out in the village or area around Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean between the Muslim and Croat populations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, between the Muslim and Croat populations in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on the 26th of January, in the morning, at 5.30 a.m., roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In January of what year, witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall where you were in the morning, early morning hours of 26 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in bed sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How were you awoken on that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was woken up by my mother. She had panicked hearing the shooting around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you do after waking up or after being awakened by your mother?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I got up. I went outside. And from the surrounding hills there were bursts of fire on the house and the holes can still be seen on the building that were made then. And we all panicked. We didn't know what to do. My mother and father were in the house, my family. So we wondered what we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you go anywhere that morning, Witness, early -- in the early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of minutes later a relative arrived who was coming from Zvonko Rajic and he said that we had been attacked, that we should all gather at the billiard room at Srecko Kristo's in the immediate neighbourhood where we used to get together anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the billiard room also known as a coffee bar or a place where you could gather for coffee?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the locals knew of it. It's an ordinary village pub. We used to gather there. A neighbour of ours ran it, and everyone knew of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you -- when you arrived at this billiard room or coffee bar, were there other people already present there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived there, together with my brother, we found our neighbours and friends who had already arrived who were also in a panic and full of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these neighbours and friends all members of the HVO, the local HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Just then when I arrived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what you were wearing and whether you were armed at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was wearing what I had at home. Actually, I put on a camouflage pants and camouflage shirt and a civilian jacket that I wore at the time, and I had been issued a Kalashnikov because we received order from Zvonko that we should all rally there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were the other HVO soldiers who were present that morning similarly dressed and similarly armed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, depending on what each person had been issued with, he brought it with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was Zvonko Rajic present when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, he wasn't, but a couple of minutes later he appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall approximately what time you arrived at the billiard room or coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was about fifteen or ten to 6.00, around 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did the group of soldiers who were in the coffee bar that morning then do? What did you do that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were surprised. We were in a state of panic. And there was an atmosphere of uncertainty as to what should be done. Zvonko tried to get in touch with Busovaca. He had a Motorola, a radio station, but it was difficult to make connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did Zvonko Rajic order the soldiers in that billiard room or coffee bar to go anywhere that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He received a report that the shooting we had heard was from the fighting on Dusina hill and that there were quite a number of dead and wounded, and he required of us that we find two volunteers who would go up there to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the geographic reference or the distance between Lasva and Dusina.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lasva, or where our houses are, is close to the station. It's a valley. And the Dusina -- Dusina and the hill is an elevation, so it's -- if you were watching from a tower, you would see us at the bottom. And the distance is about 3 kilometres between Dusina and Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is the 3 kilometres going via the road, or would that be cross-country or in a straight line?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, along the road. The distance by road is up to 3 kilometres. But as the crow flies, it's much closer. You can see the houses. You can even see the people walking in front of their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is the approximate distance between Lasva and Dusina as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't tell you exactly what the distance is in a straight line, but as I was saying, you could see easily people working in their fields in front of their houses. I could see them from my house, a part of it actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that Zvonko Rajic requested two volunteers to go to Dusina to see what was going on. In fact, did two individuals volunteer to go to Dusina that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is true, yes. Zvonko was looking for volunteers. However, people were panicking and were fearful, and while we hesitated no one had the courage to say, "I'll go," and then simply "we'll all go and we'll suffer the same fate for better or for worse." In the meantime, while we were discussing this, we decided to go. And as we tried to leave the coffee bar, fire was opened, so we turned back. We went back inside. And we were horrified and didn't know what to do. Zvonko said that we had to get out somehow. Then we tried getting out again; again fire was opened at us. And then we saw two soldiers who were fully armed, in combat gear, and they were shooting at them as well as at us, so we had to go back in again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. You told us that you saw two soldiers who were fully armed in combat gear. Were those soldiers that were fully armed and in combat gear also members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One gentleman was from Visoko, and he was of Muslim faith; and the other gentleman was from Nemila, also of Muslim faith. They had camouflage uniform on them. They were armed especially well, and they had green ribbons across their foreheads with Arab letters on them, and the other one had such a ribbon on his right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the soldiers who were firing at your unit, your HVO unit, were they from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were on the surrounding hills around our houses, because as I was saying, we're in a valley, so our houses were lined -- formed a line. They were standing one next to the other, the houses inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you saw these two armed Muslim soldiers approaching on the road, did you or anyone from your unit fire at them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We called them inside, and they came inside with us, in the coffee bar, where we were. And when they entered -- again, armed to the teeth -- the people were terrified because we had markings of the HVO on our uniforms, so we realised that they were -- belonged to a different army. They had somehow lost their way amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know why your unit did not open fire on these two Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no reason to. These boys were going along the road, and we were quite confused. We didn't know what was happening. We knew that a day earlier fighting had started around Busovaca between Muslim and Croat forces, but we were neutral. We didn't interfere in that at all. That was Zvonko's order. He wouldn't allow the slightest excess. So there was no reason. These guys, these soldiers, were also confused and they came inside to seek shelter. They were in shock too. There was no point in shooting at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you see any specific markings other than the Arab script that you've talked about, any unit patches or any markings on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: These two soldiers who were there, on them I didn't. The only thing I could see was these green ribbons around their heads with Arabic script. And we sat there together and spoke to them in this coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you talk to them about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Out of fear and curiosity we were asking what was going on. They didn't seem to know. They were confused, because we were soldiers whom they were supposed to attack, and they were confused. At first they didn't believe anything, because they too were shocked. They had expected us to resist, that a conflict would break out or that we would mistreat them or something. That was their initial impression. They were under stress. After a certain amount of time, when we started talking and when we asked them what was going on, these guys couldn't understand. They asked us how many inhabitants we were, where we were living, how, and so on. When we told them how many of us were living there, they simply couldn't believe it. They had been told that we were some sort of a major force, that we had tanks, that we had special detachments, special units, and things that didn't make any sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did they give you, during the course of this conversation, did they give you any indication as to the size of their force?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked themselves why they had to have so many soldiers there against the 50 or 60 households that you numbered. They were in shock too. They just couldn't believe it themselves. They just couldn't believe that things were happening as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many soldiers they spoke about when they were talking amongst themselves, how many soldiers they had?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't give an exact figure and say exactly how many soldiers they were, but they did mention units, what did so many units of the brigade -- what were they there for, because it was all beyond belief. That's the kind of thing they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall them indicating or saying which brigade or brigades were involved?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They mentioned the 303rd Mountain Brigade and some Visoko Brigade too, the 7th Muslim was mentioned, the Territorial Defence, the local one, then the Patriotic League, and the regular army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The units that you just named, are those all units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did belong -- well, actually, whether they were special units or some other kinds of units, they did come under the supervision of the BH army; of course, as they fought together with them. That would be natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when the HVO unit then left the coffee bar on the morning of 26 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time the unit left and where the unit went?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that conversation - I don't know how much time they spent on that - but anyway, we started out. There were some ten soldiers, ten of us, roughly speaking, and we went towards Vranjaca, passing by our houses. And we climbed up there towards the village of Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where in relation to Dusina is the village of Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a part of Dusina, in actual fact. Before you get to Dusina, there's a hamlet, and that's where there were several Croatian households. The rest, 99 per cent of them, were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the movements of your units toward the village of Brdo. What happened as you were climbing towards Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we started off moving alongside our houses and up the hill - this was mostly Croatian land - and in between the houses they opened fire at us from the surrounding hills, so that there was Krvaca [phoen], Gornja Visnjica. Those were the hills and villages and that's where they shot at us from. So we had to move from one house to the next and to a small thicket and reach the relay up on the hill, relay station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "they opened fire at us," do you know who it was that opened fire at you, which military force?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Territorial Defence. They were in those surrounding parts, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please proceed to tell us what happened when you reached the relay station, the transmitter relay station.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we reached the transmitter relay station, it was situated in a large valley, open space all around. You could see it from Dusina and from the surrounding hills. And they opened fire on us from that area using heavy weaponry and light weaponry as well. And we had to take cover under a small hill and had to crawl and make our way to the village of Brdo itself, above Radakove Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person by the name of Drago Rados?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who -- who is Drago Rados and where did he live?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Drago Rados lived at Brdo, up on the hill, and he was the commander of the department in Dusina of a squadron and -- of the military squad, the military-able men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So he was the HVO squadron commander in Dusina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if there was any communication between Zvonko Rajic and Drago Rados on the morning of 26 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think there was, because he heard Zvonko. He had a radio station, and he said that they had been attacked and that there were some people who had been killed and were dead, and also some people wounded. And he asked for help. He asked Zvonko to send help and asked him what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the HVO unit under Zvonko Rajic's command that you were a part of proceed to the house of Drago Rados in Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And we got there, above his house. There's a plum -- there's some plum trees. And Perica Rados's house is right next door. He's a family member, Perica Rados. So these were family houses. And there was -- there were some plum trees behind. But we couldn't pass because they opened fire at us. And across the road there were some Muslim houses, and that's where the BH army positions were from where they opened fire on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you reach Drago Rados on that morning? Was your unit able to physically reach Drago Rados that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We started off upwards, and as soon as we did they shot at us, so we had to go back. There was a sort of little hill. And we stood behind the plum orchard, in actual fact, took cover there. We weren't able to approach any further. We were struck by panic, didn't know what to do, because it was all very surprising to us, and we were wondering what to do next. Zvonko tried to get in touch with the command in Busovaca. He used his Motorola, but it was very difficult to establish a connection, to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time on that morning when Drago Rados was united with your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next time we set off, we decided to open fire and shoot at them this time and to try and reach Perica Rados's house, to help them to get out of there and to see what was going on generally. And we succeeded in doing that, and then Mijo Ljubicic turned up, as well as Perica Rados and Drago Rados.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time it was when you saw Drago Rados on that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was morning, early. I couldn't give you an exact time. We didn't bother to look at our watches. But it might have been sometime around 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Later that day, Witness, did you see a column of civilian people from where you were located on Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Drago Rados arrived and the other man, Perica, but they were lost, and Mijo Ljubicic said that his father had -- "My father had been killed and lay in front of the house dead," and he also said that he saw an old man by the name of Rados too - we didn't know his surname referred to him as Cica - that he lay there dead on the spot where he had been killed, and Mijo Ljubicic told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just clarify one of your answers. When Mijo Ljubicic mentioned his father -- mentioned a father being killed, was that his father, Mijo Ljubicic's father, or was that your father?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: His father, because they were in the house together. And when the shooting started, his father ran out of the house and that's where he was killed. And Mr. Mijo Ljubicic jumped out of the window and he left him there and ran to Perica's house -- Rados's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber this group of civilians that you saw that morning from Brdo.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we talked and were wondering what to do, Zvonko tried to get a connection to somebody but we were afraid, generally speaking, and at one point in time from the village of Dusina we were looking across the valley and we saw a group of people, civilians, coming along, led by soldiers with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this group walking along a road?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The road went in the opposite direction. They were moving towards our positions, where we were, and going across the meadow, the ordinary meadows and fields, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many people were in this group, how many civilian people were in this group?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were members of our family, women, children and elderly persons who had survived the Golgotha that happened at Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where were those people coming from? What village or villages were these people coming from?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were coming from -- actually, they were our neighbours. And in the evening, out of fear they grouped together in a house, because they thought that they'd be safer and they went to Marko Rajic's house, and that was at Dusina. They were in his cellar, in actual fact, and they grouped together, safety in numbers sort of thing. They thought if they were all together nothing would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So they were coming from the direction of Dusina towards the position that you were at and your unit was at on Brdo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate number of civilians in this group?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, I would say there were about 20 of them, 20 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far were these people from the position that your HVO unit was at? How far away were they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 150 to 200 metres. In an open space. They were out in a meadow, in actual fact. And the armed soldiers were there and went behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened to this group of people as they approached your position on Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They stopped behind an old house. There's a small plum orchard there. I think the man's name was Pasko. He was a local of Brdo. And they stood behind that house. And then Mr. Edin Hakanovic addressed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who is Edin Hakanovic? And did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is a gentleman who lived at Brdo. He was from Lasva originally. I know him we grew up together. And before the war, he was a policeman. He worked in Visoko as a policeman. He attended some sort of course. He was a civil engineer and then underwent some training and found employment as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From the position that you were at on Brdo, could you hear what Edin Hakanovic was saying to the group of civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us a few moments ago that the group of people, the civilians, stopped in a plum orchard and that Edin Hakanovic addressed them. From your position on Brdo, could you hear what he was saying to them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand. He didn't address the civilians, actually. He was calling to Zvonko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So Edin Hakanovic was addressing Zvonko Rajic, who was with you and the HVO unit on Brdo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We were lying down next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did Edin Hakanovic say to Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: He said that he should come out and that they should give themselves up and that then they would stop shooting and that we ought to negotiate. That's what he asked Zvonko to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How far away was Edin Hakanovic was he was saying this to Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 100 metres. If you spoke up, you could hear what the other man was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point in time, did Zvonko Rajic enter into negotiations with Edin Hakanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Zvonko did try to negotiate and ask Edin what was happening, what they were doing, and Mr. Hakanovic said that he would send Drago Rados's wife to explain to us so he didn't have to shout it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In fact, did Drago Rados's wife then approach your HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They let her cross the field and reach our positions. They stopped shooting. Nobody shot at us then while this was going on. So she came up to us and the woman was in shock. She was completely beside herself. And the first words she said, "They'll kill us all." And she said that massacres had started at Dusina and that they had killed all the civilians and military-able men, that they had taken people out from Marko Rajic's cellar and had shot them. And she also said that if -- unless Zvonko surrenders, they would all be killed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point in time, did Zvonko Rajic in fact surrender?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. She had to go back. And we were still there, lost, didn't know what to do next. And Zvonko didn't want to decide anything on his own. He once again tried to reach the main command in Busovaca on his Motorola. And in one of those attempts he was successful and did get a line through to the command, and the commanding officer ordered Zvonko to negotiate and to do everything possible to see that people weren't killed and that he should do that at any price and that they would do their best to send UN observers to provide us with some degree of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did Zvonko Rajic do after receiving this order from his commander in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko was at a loss what to do. It was minus 5 degrees and yet he was sweating. He couldn't speak. And he asked me to call Edin up again. And that's what I did, of course. And Edin responded to my call. Zvonko asked him to give guarantees that he wouldn't harm anyone and that they should all go to the schoolhouse, the school building, and the local community in Lasva, where meetings were usually held and where they would communicate, and that they should go and have some negotiations. That's what Edin asked them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did Zvonko Rajic do after Edin Hakanovic told him this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Edin Hakanovic did issue guarantees. He said there'd be no problems for him to come and that he could start out quite safely across the field and meadow to where he was, to where Zvonko was. And Zvonko asked us whether any of us would volunteer to go with him so as not to go alone. We all kept quiet. We were all silent. Of course, everybody was afraid after what we had just heard from Drago's wife as to what had happened and what was going on generally, so nobody had the courage to come forward and go along with him. Then Ivica Filipovic said, "Zvonko can't go on his own. One of us has to go." And then Franjo Batinic got up and volunteered to go with him. So hid Perica Rados, he said he would accompany him too. And Drago Rados stood up too, as well as Kristo Jozo and Srecko Kristo. They all volunteered to go with him, as well as Viktor Kristo, who was Zvonko's brother. So they all volunteered to go with him, with Zvonko. I was next to Zvonko and Velimir Kristo too, and he asked the two of us to go with him as well. I refused. I didn't dare go, because I said I didn't believe them, that I thought they'd kill us all anyway. Then Zvonko got up and told Edin that he was on his way. Once they all got up and walked across the field, Edin said that they should take the bullets out of the barrel - because, of course, they all had rifles - and that he guaranteed that nothing would happen to them. And that's what they did, and started off towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, after this group of six or seven individuals followed Zvonko Rajic, you told us that you remained on the hill. How many other HVO soldiers remained with you on the hill, as the others went down towards Edin Hakanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Seven of eight of us -- seven or eight of us. And Zvonko said, when he set off, "If you notice anything, we'll kill them and not let them be taken alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "we'll kill them," who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: To Zvonko and the other guys that went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so I understand, witness, are you telling us that Zvonko told you and the remaining men on the hill to shoot them, to shoot at Zvonko and the other HVO soldiers if it appeared that they were going to be taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not to be taken away. If they harmed them at all, that we should kill them. That's what Zvonko asked us to do. I and Velo Kristo stayed on, Kresimir Kristo stayed too, Ivica Kristo, and several others, Zdeno Kristo. There were about eight of us. I can't remember all their names, because there was general panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, at this point in time, the group of civilians that you had seen, did they remain in the meadow down by the plum orchard, or did they go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they stayed on in the meadow right up until they reached Edin and the road leading that way to Edin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did they go once they reached the road and Edin Hakanovic? Where did the civilians go?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When Zvonko and the six other soldiers who were with him, when they reached Edin Hakanovic, it was the road above Drago Rados's house, that's where they stopped. And when, from the surrounding houses members of the BH army came out who were there - they were armed - and they disarmed Zvonko and the six soldiers. After that, the civilians were taken down the meadow, the field, they were taken to the road -- the main road leading towards Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened to the group that went with Zvonko Rajic to negotiate with Edin Hakanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: When they got a couple of metres from Edin, the soldiers came behind their backs, surrounded them, disarmed them, took their weapons from them, forced them to raise their heads behind -- hands behind their heads. They took Zvonko's bag, radio station. I think he had a pistol on him; they took that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did they remain there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not for long, a couple of minutes. They took them along the road then, downhill towards Lasva. We were watching from above and not knowing what to do. We panicked and we were following to see where they would take them. Close to Edin's house there's a road leading towards the relay. They stopped there for a moment. We could hear arguments and shouts, and they took them along that road. Then we heard a shot, again some shouting and arguing, and this took a couple of minutes roughly, maybe 15 or 20 minutes. After that, we saw them again coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, witness. After 15 or 20 minutes, you then saw them coming back up the hill from Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They hadn't left the village of Brdo really. They had just moved away from the water a couple of hundred metres away. Some quarreling started there, shouting. We heard a shot. They stayed there for 15 or 20 minutes, and then they turned back from -- to the same position where they had started from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say "the same position that they had started from," that's the same position where Zvonko Rajic initially went down to discuss issues with Edin Hakanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, near the trough where they kept them, where they had held them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. We feel that these are leading questions for the witness; that the Prosecution is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. Rephrase your question so it is less leading, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, where was Zvonko Rajic at the time you say that he returned?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko didn't return. They were carrying him. He had been wounded in the thigh. I think it was of his right leg. He was being carried by Franjo Batinic, his brother Drago, and Perica Rados. This was after this shot and after the argument, when they were coming back. Zvonko wasn't walking; he was being carried, because he had been wounded in his thigh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where were you at the time when you saw this, witness?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I and the other members with me were in the same spot. We hadn't moved, where we had been negotiating, in the meadow, a very specific spot. It's an elevation, so we could see everything that was happening below us. Below us was a kind of valley, along which went the road and the stream flowing past these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far were you at that point from Zvonko Rajic and the other group?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but in a straight line maybe 50 to 70 metres away, not more. We could clearly see one another and recognise one another. I told you a moment ago if you spoke loudly, you could hear the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the point in time when you saw Zvonko Rajic having been injured could you hear any conversations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could hear moans, saying that he was in pain. He asked Edin whether -- "Is this your guarantee? What's going on?" We heard all that. And after that they reached this trough and they put Zvonko into this mud, into this water; that is, the soldiers who were with him were forced to place their hands behind their heads and to look into the ground, look down in front of Zvonko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many ABiH soldiers were with Edin Hakanovic at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a number of them around them, about ten or so. And then we saw a group of five or six soldiers coming from one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these -- were these ABiH soldiers or HVO soldiers that you saw coming from one side?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A gentleman was among them who had flak jackets and boys were with him wearing green camouflage uniforms and black vests and they had ribbons around their heads, as I described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who any of these ABiH soldiers that you saw approaching from the side, do you know the identity of any of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just then I didn't know, but we could hear what was being said. We were watching all this. Zvonko was lying there wounded, and he was bleeding profusely and he recognised among the approaching soldiers a gentleman, and he asked him to give him first aid, to take him to see a doctor. However, they started laughing and ridiculing him, and then the mistreatment started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific with respect to the mistreatment that you mentioned. Can you tell us what type of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was mistreatment. Zvonko was on the ground. He was being kicked. Then this man who had come with this group, he took out his Skorpion pistol, an automatic pistol, he turned towards Zvonko and said that he would give him first aid and he shot him in the head, a burst of fire, and then he turned around. Right next to Zvonko was Drago Rados. When he had fired the bullets at Zvonko, he pointed the pistol at Drago's forehead and fired. There were no more bullets left. He said, "It is Allah's will," and those around him were saying, "Tekbir" and "Allah-u-ekber."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when Zvonko Rajic was shot, how far away were you at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the same spot, and not just I, in the same position where Zvonko used to be, where we were negotiating from. We didn't move from that spot. And this was about, as I said, 50 to 70 metres away in a straight line. We were watching this; as I was saying, we were on a slightly higher level, so we could see everything below. And the gentlemen, the guys who were with Zvonko, thanks to God, are all six of them alive. They were watching this. And after that, their hands were tied behind their backs and they were taken away towards the canyon, that is, along the edge of the wood, in the opposite direction than Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko -- Mr. Zvonko remained lying there in the mud.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened, as you witnessed this -- can you describe for the Chamber what happened to Zvonko Rajic as he was shot?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He remained there lying dead, and after that we were still standing up there. We didn't know what to do. He was still lying there. They scattered. They went searching the houses to see whether there was anyone left behind. We were in the bushes in the meadow. Just then we panicked. We didn't know what to do. And Dragan Kristo appeared, who came up to us and he conveyed to us that we had to go down to the school to surrender all of us, that he had met civilians and that all the people at Dusina had been killed and unless all of us go there, that they would kill all the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if I could just interrupt you. Do you know -- to return briefly to the incident involving Zvonko Rajic. The person who shot Zvonko Rajic, do you know his identity?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Serif Patkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you know Serif Patkovic from prior to the war, or had you ever seen him before the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know the gentleman personally, but he had negotiated with Zvonko, so I knew who he was, and I knew that he was a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade -- or rather, that he was in command of that unit; we learnt that. And before, when these incidents had occurred, numerous problems related to Zvonko, I wasn't close to the man but I knew what he looked like and who he was. After this, after it was all over in Dusina, when Dragan reached us, this same gentleman came to the school and called out our names, the man who had killed Zvonko. And he introduced himself, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall approximately how far Serif Patkovic was standing from Zvonko Rajic when he shot him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was just above his head. In fact, he was pressing his wound with his leg and then he emptied his pistol into his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, witness, you mentioned a few moments ago being in a school. Did you in fact go to a school on the 26th of January, 1993 after witnessing Zvonko Rajic being murdered?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't go to the school straight away. The soldiers who were there, when Dragan arrived, we went down along the same path we had taken coming there. We went back to the coffee bar, the billiard, where these two soldiers were that we had left behind belonging to the BH army, and also our elderly men who had sought shelter there and the guys who had stayed behind in the village, who were in their houses and hadn't come to join us and who later arrived at the coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. Obviously I'm not going to finish this witness today. I anticipate having approximately 15 minutes of questioning for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] So, witness, you shall return tomorrow and we shall begin the hearing at 9.00 tomorrow morning and you will be cross-examined for a quarter of an hour and we will ask you to contact neither the Defence nor the Prosecution teams when you have finished and once you've left the courtroom today. It is now quarter to 2.00. This hearing is now adjourned and shall resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: 1.46 p.m., to be resumed on Wednesday, the 3rd day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
